awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for the 2025 Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK)
awd_abstract_narration:
This project seeks a travel grant to support student attendance at the 2025 Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK) in Taipei, Taiwan. ESWEEK is a premier international event that unites leading conferences in embedded systems and software, covering critical advancements in compilers, architectures, hardware/software codesign, and embedded software development. Supporting student participation in ESWEEK directly serves the national interest by fostering the next generation of innovators in a field crucial for advancing technology, prosperity, and welfare. Increased student attendance will enrich the conference and help attract students from all background to embedded systems and STEM research. Students will gain unique opportunities to interact with global experts and industry leaders, discuss their research, and establish connections vital for their professional careers. This initiative aims to address financial barriers that often prevent students from attending, thereby ensuring a more skilled workforce for the future of embedded systems.

The project's goal is to provide travel support for approximately 30 eligible students to attend ESWEEK 2025. Eligibility is restricted to undergraduate or graduate students currently enrolled at a U.S. university, including U.S. citizens traveling from other countries. Priority for funding will be given to students presenting their research work at ESWEEK, its symposia, and workshops, with a special preference for U.S. citizens and permanent residents. The grant will cover a portion of reimbursable expenses, including airfare (on U.S.-flag carriers or ticketed through U.S. carriers), ground transportation, lodging, registration fees, and meals. Outreach for travel support will be widely advertised through the ESWEEK website, mailing lists, and technical society newsletters. Student applications will be collected via email, requiring a resume, a cover letter detailing reasons for attending and estimated expenses, and an advisor's letter supporting the application and stating other funding availability. A committee will select awardees based on eligibility, participation level, research alignment, advisor recommendation, and prioritizing U.S. students. After the event, each awarded student must submit a one-page report on their impressions and outcomes.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Embedded computing systems are the computers we rarely think about: the processors inside medical devices, automobiles, aircraft, industrial equipment, smartphones, and the growing array of sensors that monitor everything from bridges to crops. Unlike desktop computers or data centers, these systems must operate under tight constraints on size, power, cost, heat, and reliability, often while making decisions in real time and without human supervision. Designing them well requires expertise that spans both hardware and software, and the field advances largely through a small number of highly selective international conferences where new results are first presented and debated.

Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK) is the premier annual event in this field. It brings together three leading conferences covering compilers and computer architecture, hardware/software co-design, and embedded software, along with a symposium on formal verification and a range of workshops, tutorials, and educational lectures. The conferences are competitive, typically accepting roughly one in four submitted papers, and the meeting draws several hundred researchers from universities, industry, and government laboratories worldwide. For a graduate student working in this field, attending ESWEEK is often the single most valuable professional experience of the year.

This award addressed a practical barrier to that experience: cost. ESWEEK 2025 was held in Taipei, Taiwan, from September 28 to October 3, 2025. International travel places the meeting out of reach for many students whose research groups cannot cover airfare, lodging, and registration, and the students most affected are frequently those from institutions with smaller research budgets. Without targeted support, participation in the field’s central scientific forum risks becoming a function of institutional wealth rather than of research merit.

With support from this award, seven graduate students from six U.S. universities attended ESWEEK 2025. The recipients came from Washington State University, the University of Southern California, The Ohio State University, Arizona State University, the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and the University of Arizona. The support would genuinely cover the cost of international travel rather than defray a fraction of it. Applications were reviewed with attention to the student’s role in the technical program, the range of institutions represented, and demonstrated financial need.

The intellectual merit of this investment lies in how research in this field actually progresses. Scientific results in embedded systems are refined through direct technical exchange: a student presenting a poster receives detailed critique from researchers who have spent decades on related problems, learns which assumptions will not survive scrutiny, and discovers parallel work that reshapes the direction of a dissertation. These exchanges are difficult to replicate remotely. By enabling students to present and defend their work in person, the award contributed to the quality and pace of research across seven distinct research programs.

The broader impacts extend in several directions. First, the award supported the development of the next generation of U.S. researchers in a technology area with direct consequences for transportation safety, medical devices, energy infrastructure, and national competitiveness in semiconductor and computing technology. The professional relationships students form at meetings like ESWEEK frequently shape where they work and what problems they choose to pursue.

Second, by distributing awards across institutions rather than concentrating them, the project helped ensure that participation in the field’s flagship conference reflected research contribution rather than institutional resources. Students from universities without large travel budgets were able to present alongside peers from the best-resourced programs.

Third, because ESWEEK 2025 was held in Asia, supported students engaged with a segment of the international embedded systems community that is less well represented at meetings held in the United States. They encountered research groups, industrial practitioners, and technical approaches they would not have met otherwise. For early-career researchers, exposure to how a problem is framed differently in another research culture has lasting value, and the international connections formed may support future collaboration.

Travel support was disbursed to seven students, each of whom attended the full conference, participated in the technical program, and engaged with the international research community. The award demonstrates that a modest and well-targeted investment in student travel can meaningfully broaden who participates in the central scientific conversations of a technical field.
